  14. <hr>
  15. <p>title: &quot;PEN-200 Module 21 \u2014 Active Directory Enumeration Primer&quot;
  16. slug: ad-enum
  17. author: m4xx3d0ut
  18. summary: Active Directory (AD) enumeration underpins every later chapter. These notes
  19. incorporate the full checklist recorded during the labs.
  20. publishedAt: &#39;2023-11-27&#39;
  21. updatedAt: &#39;2024-01-07&#39;
  22. readingMinutes: 144
  23. tags:</p>
  24. <ul>
  25. <li>offsec</li>
  26. </ul>
  27. <hr>
  28. <h2>TLDR;</h2>
  29. <p>Active Directory (AD) enumeration underpins every later chapter. These notes incorporate the full checklist recorded during the labs.</p>
  30. <h3>Baseline Footprinting</h3>
  31. <pre><code>nltest /dsgetdc:corp.local
  32. nltest /dclist:corp.local
  33. net config workstation
  34. net accounts /domain
  35. Get-ADDomain | Select-Object Name,DomainMode,ForestMode
  36. </code></pre>
  37. <ul>
  38. <li>Document domain functional level, FSMO roles, and trust relationships.</li>
  39. <li>Capture DNS zone transfers (<code>dnstool.py</code>) and GPO links.</li>
  40. </ul>
  41. <h3>LDAP &amp; SMB Recon</h3>
  42. <pre><code>ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.corp.local -D &#39;corp\ldapsvc&#39; -w &#39;Passw0rd!&#39; -b &#39;DC=corp,DC=local&#39; &#39;(objectClass=user)&#39; sAMAccountName userAccountControl
  43. ldapsearch -x -H ldap://dc01.corp.local -b &#39;DC=corp,DC=local&#39; &#39;(servicePrincipalName=*)&#39; sAMAccountName servicePrincipalName
  44. ​
  45. smbmap -H fileserver.corp.local -u backupuser -p &#39;Passw0rd!&#39;
  46. net view \\fileserver /all
  47. </code></pre>
  48. <ul>
  49. <li>Track accounts with <code>adminCount=1</code>, disabled status, or interesting descriptions.</li>
  50. <li>Enumerate shares, permissions, and accessible directories.</li>
  51. </ul>
  52. <h3>Automated Graphing</h3>
  53. <pre><code># Collectors
  54. Invoke-BloodHound -CollectionMethod All,GPOLocalGroup -Domain corp.local -ZipFile .\loot\bh.zip
  55. bloodhound-python -c All -u analyst -p &#39;Passw0rd!&#39; -d corp.local -gc dc01.corp.local
  56. </code></pre>
  57. <ul>
  58. <li>Import into BloodHound, run queries (“Shortest path to Domain Admins”, “Find all Kerberoastable Accounts”).</li>
  59. <li>Screenshot key graphs for the report and log collection timestamps.</li>
  60. </ul>
  61. <h3>Credential Hygiene Checks</h3>
  62. <ul>
  63. <li><code>Get-ADUser -Filter {PasswordNeverExpires -eq $true}</code>.</li>
  64. <li><code>Get-ADFineGrainedPasswordPolicy</code> to see if weak policies exist.</li>
  65. <li>Identify unconstrained/ constrained delegation: <code>Get-ADComputer -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true}</code>.</li>
  66. <li>Note service accounts with weak SPNs and tier-0 group members.</li>
  67. </ul>
  68. <h3>Reporting Data Points</h3>
  69. <ul>
  70. <li>Build a table of high-risk findings: missing SMB signing, outdated functional level, excessive Domain Admin membership.</li>
  71. <li>Provide remediation guidance: enforce LDAP signing, enable Protected Users group, rotate service account passwords to gMSA.</li>
  72. </ul>
  73. <p>Comprehensive AD enumeration now will save you hours when you start roasting, relaying, and moving laterally in Modules 22–24.</p>
  74. <h2>Working Notes... In Graphic Detail...</h2>
  75. <h3>Active Directory Introduction and Enumeration</h3>
  76. <ul>
  77. <li>Introduction to Active Directory.</li>
  78. <li>Active Directory enumeration using manual tools.</li>
  79. <li>Enumerating Active Directory using automated tools.</li>
  80. </ul>
  81. <p><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/virtual-dc/active-directory-domain-services-overview">Active Directory Domain Services</a></p>
  82. <h4>21.1 Active Directory - Introduction</h4>
  83. <ul>
  84. <li>Introduction to Active Directory.</li>
  85. <li>Define our enumeration goals.</li>
  86. </ul>
  87. <p>AD contains critival info about the env, reffered to as objects.</p>
  88. <ul>
  89. <li>User info.</li>
  90. <li>Groups.</li>
  91. <li>Computers.</li>
  92. </ul>
  93. <p>Configuring/maintaining an AD instance can be daunting, the wealth of info creates a large attack surface.</p>
  94. <p>The first step in AD config is creating a domain name, <code>corp.com</code> for instance, which is often the name of the org itself. Within the domain, admins can add various objects associated with the org.</p>
  95. <p><em>An AD environment has a critical dependency on the Domain Name System (DNS) service. As such, a typical domain controller will also host a DNS server that is authoritative for a given domain.</em></p>
  96. <p>To ease object and system management, admins organize the objects into <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organizational_unit_(computing)">Organizational Units (OUs)</a>.</p>
  97. <p>OUs are like file system folders, they are containers used to store objects within a domain. Computer objects represent actual servers and workstations that are domain-joined and user objects represent accounts that can be used to log into domain-joined computers. AD objects contain attributes which will vary depending on the type of object. A user object may include attributes such as first name, last name, username, phone number, etc.</p>
  98. <p>AD relies on several components and communication services. When a user logs in, a request is sent to a Domain Controller (DC), that checks if the user is allowed to log in to the domain. One or more DCs act as the core of the domain and store all OUs, objects, and their attributes. Since the DC is a central component, we pay close attention to it while we enumerate AD.</p>
  99. <p>Objects can be assigned to AD groups so that admins can manage them as a single unit. Users in a group can be given access to a file server share or granted admin access to various clients in the domain. Attackers often target high-priv groups.</p>
  100. <p>Domain Admin members are among the highest priv objects in the domain. If an attacker compromises a member of this group, often reffered to as &quot;domain administrators&quot;, they essentially gain full control over the domain.</p>
  101. <p>This vector could extend beyond a single domain since an AD instance can host more than one domain in a domain tree or multiple domain trees in a domain forest. There are Domain Admin groups for each domain in the forest, members of the Enterprise Admins group are granted full control over all the domains in the forest and have Admin privs on all DCs, making them a high value target.</p>
  102. <p>We will leverage these and other concepts in this moduleas we focus on the important aspects of AD enumeration. This important discipline can improve our success during the attack phase. We will leverage a variety of tools to manually enumerate AD, most rely on the <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lightweight_Directory_Access_Protocol">Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP)</a>. Once we&#39;ve introduced foundational techniques, we&#39;ll leverage automation to perform enumeration at scale.</p>
  103. <h5>Enumeration - Defining our Goals</h5>
  104. <p>In this scenario we will enumerate <code>corp.com</code> domain. We&#39;ve obtained user credentials to a domain user through a successful phishing attack. Alternatively, the org may have provided us with user creds so that we can perform a pentest base on an assumed breach. This would speed up the process and give the org insight into how easily attackers can move within their enc once they have gained initial access.</p>
  105. <p>the user we have is <code>stephanie</code> who has RDP perms on a Win 11 machine that is part of the domain. the user is not a local admin on the machine, which we take into account as we proceed.</p>
  106. <p>During a real-world, the org may also define the scope and goals of the pentest. In our case, we are restricted to the <code>corp.com</code> domain with the PWK labs. Our goal will be to enumerate the full domain, including ways to achieve the highest priv possible, domain admin in this case.</p>
  107. <p>In this module, we will perform the enumeration from a client machine with the low priv <code>stephanie</code> user. Once we start performing attacks and we are able to gain access to additional users/systems, we may have to repeat parts of the enumeration process from the new postiion. Perspective shift, or pivot, is critical during the enum process considering the complexity of permissions across the domain. Each pivot may give us an opportunity to advance our attack.</p>
  108. <p>For example, if we gain another low priv user account that has the seems to have the same access as <code>stephanie</code> we shouldn&#39;t dismiss it. Instead, we should repeat enumeration with the new account since the admins often grant individual users increased perms based on their role in the org. This &quot;rinse and repeat&quot; process is key to success in enumeration and works extremely well, particularly in large orgs.</p>
  109. <h4>21.2 Active Directory - Manual Enumeration</h4>
  110. <ul>
  111. <li>Enumerate Active Directory using legacy Windows applications.</li>
  112. <li>Use PowerShell and .NET to perform additional AD enumeration.</li>
  113. </ul>
  114. <h5>Active Directory - Enumeration Using Legacy Windows Tools</h5>
  115. <p>Since we are in an assumed breach scenario and we have creds for <code>stephanie</code>, we will use those creds to auth to the domain via Win 11 machine <code>CLIENT75</code>. Use RDP with <code>xfreerdp</code> to connect to the client and log in to the domain.</p>
  116. <ul>
  117. <li>User <code>/u</code></li>
  118. <li>Domain <code>/d</code></li>
  119. <li>Password <code>LegmanTeamBenzoin!!</code></li>
  120. </ul>
  121. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec]
  122. └─$ xfreerdp /u:stephanie /d:corp.com /v:192.168.227.75
  123. </code></pre>
  124. <p>AD contains enourmous amounts of information, it can be hard to determine where to start enumerating. Since every AD install contains users and groups, we start there.</p>
  125. <p>Start gathering user info with <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-US/troubleshoot/windows-server/networking/net-commands-on-operating-systems">net.exe</a>, installed by default on all Win OS systems. Specifically we will use the <code>net user</code> sub-command. As we know, we can use this tool to enum local accounts onthe machine, we&#39;ll use the <code>/domain</code> to print out users on the domain.</p>
  126. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\stephanie&gt;net user /domain
  127. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  128. ​
  129. ​
  130. User accounts for \\DC1.corp.com
  131. ​
  132. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  133. Administrator dave Guest
  134. iis_service jeff jeffadmin
  135. jen krbtgt pete
  136. stephanie
  137. The command completed successfully.
  138. </code></pre>
  139. <ul>
  140. <li>The output will vary depending on the size of the org.</li>
  141. <li>We can now query info about individual users.</li>
  142. </ul>
  143. <p>Admins have a tendancy to add prefix or suffix to usernames that identify accounts by their function. Based on the output, we should check out the <code>jeffadmin</code> user because it may be an admin account.</p>
  144. <p>Inspect with <code>net.exe</code> and the <code>/domain</code> flag.</p>
  145. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\stephanie&gt;net user jeffadmin /domain
  146. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  147. ​
  148. User name jeffadmin
  149. Full Name
  150. Comment
  151. User&#39;s comment
  152. Country/region code 000 (System Default)
  153. Account active Yes
  154. Account expires Never
  155. ​
  156. Password last set 9/2/2022 3:26:48 PM
  157. Password expires Never
  158. Password changeable 9/3/2022 3:26:48 PM
  159. Password required Yes
  160. User may change password Yes
  161. ​
  162. Workstations allowed All
  163. Logon script
  164. User profile
  165. Home directory
  166. Last logon 9/27/2023 5:08:57 AM
  167. ​
  168. Logon hours allowed All
  169. ​
  170. Local Group Memberships *Administrators
  171. Global Group memberships *Domain Users *Domain Admins
  172. The command completed successfully.
  173. </code></pre>
  174. <ul>
  175. <li><code>jeffadmin</code> is a part of the <code>Domain Admins</code> group, which we take note of.</li>
  176. <li>If we compromise this account we elevate to domain admin.</li>
  177. </ul>
  178. <p>We can also use <code>net.exe</code> to enum groups in the domain with <code>net group</code>.</p>
  179. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\stephanie&gt;net group /domain
  180. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  181. ​
  182. ​
  183. Group Accounts for \\DC1.corp.com
  184. ​
  185. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  186. *Cloneable Domain Controllers
  187. *Debug
  188. *Development Department
  189. *DnsUpdateProxy
  190. *Domain Admins
  191. *Domain Computers
  192. *Domain Controllers
  193. *Domain Guests
  194. *Domain Users
  195. *Enterprise Admins
  196. *Enterprise Key Admins
  197. *Enterprise Read-only Domain Controllers
  198. *Group Policy Creator Owners
  199. *Key Admins
  200. *Management Department
  201. *Protected Users
  202. *Read-only Domain Controllers
  203. *Sales Department
  204. *Schema Admins
  205. The command completed successfully.
  206. </code></pre>
  207. <ul>
  208. <li>Some of these are <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-groups">default</a></li>
  209. <li>Others are custom groups created by the admin, which we enum first.</li>
  210. <li>Sales Department.</li>
  211. <li>Management Department.</li>
  212. <li>Development Department.</li>
  213. </ul>
  214. <p>We use <code>net</code> again to enum group members, focusing on Sales Department.</p>
  215. <pre><code class="language-powershell">C:\Users\stephanie&gt;net group &quot;Sales Department&quot; /domain
  216. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  217. ​
  218. Group name Sales Department
  219. Comment
  220. ​
  221. Members
  222. ​
  223. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  224. pete stephanie
  225. The command completed successfully.
  226. </code></pre>
  227. <ul>
  228. <li>We find <code>pete</code> and <code>stephanie</code> are members of the Sales Department group.</li>
  229. </ul>
  230. <p>In real-world, enum each group and catalog the results. This requires good organization, which we will discuss later, but we for now we will move on to more flexible alternatives to <code>net.exe</code>.</p>

  654. <h5>Enumerating Active Directory using PowerShell and .NET Classes</h5>
  655. <p>We have several tools for AD enum. PowerShell cmdlets like <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/get-aduser?view=windowsserver2022-ps">Get-ADUser</a> work well but are only installed by default on domain controller as part of the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/windows-server/system-management-components/remote-server-administration-tools">Remote Server Administration Tools (RSAT)</a>. RSAT is rarely present on domain clients and we need admin privs to install them. We can, in principal, impor the DLL required for enum ourselves, but we will look into other options.</p>
  656. <p>We&#39;ll develop a tool that requires only basic privs and is flexible enough to use in real-world. We will mimic the queries AD uses under regular operation. This will help us understand the basic concepts used in pre-built tools we&#39;ll use later.</p>
  657. <p>We&#39;ll use PowerShell and .NET classes to create a script that enums the domain. Although PS development can be complex, we will take it one step at a time.</p>
  658. <p>To enum AD, we first need to understand how to comm with the service. Before we start writing our script, we will discuss some theory.</p>
  659. <p>AD enum relies on LDAP. When a domain machine searches for an object, like a printer, or when we query user/group objects, LDAP is used as the comm channel for the query. In other words, LDAP is the proto used to comm with AD.</p>
  660. <p><em>LDAP is not exclusive to AD. Other directory services use it as well.</em></p>
  661. <p>LDAP comm with AD is not always straight-forward, but we can leverage <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/adsi/active-directory-service-interfaces-adsi">Active Directory Services Interface (ADSI)</a> as an LDAP provider.</p>
  662. <p>According to MS docs, we need a specific LDAP ADsPath to comm with AD service. LDAP path prototype looks like:</p>
  663. <pre><code>LDAP://HostName[:PortNumber][/DistinguishedName]
  664. </code></pre>
  665. <ul>
  666. <li>We need 3 params for the full LDAP path.</li>
  667. <li>HostName.</li>
  668. <li>PortNumber.</li>
  669. <li>DistinguishedName.</li>
  670. </ul>
  671. <p>Hostname can be a computer name, IP address, or a domain name. In our case, we are working with the <code>corp.com</code> domain, so we can simply add that to our LDAP path and likely obtain info. Note that a domain may have multiple DCs, so setting the domain name could resolve to the IP address of any DC in the domain.</p>
  672. <p>While this will return valid info, it may not be the optimal approach. In fact, to make out enum as accurate as possible, we should look for the DC that holds the most current info. This is know as the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-GB/troubleshoot/windows-server/identity/fsmo-roles">Primary Domain Controller (PDC)</a>. There can only be one PDC in a domain. To find the PDC, we need to find the DC holding the <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> property. We&#39;ll use PowerShell and a specific .NET class to find this.</p>
  673. <p>The PortNumber for LDAP conn is options per MS docs. In this case, we will not add the port number since it will auto choose the port based on if we are using SSL or not. It is worth noting that if we come across a domain using non-default ports, we may need to manually add this to the script.</p>
  674. <p>The <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/desktop/ldap/distinguished-names">DistinguishedName (DN)</a> is part of the LDAP path. A DN is a name that uniquely identifies an object in AD, including the domain itself. If we aren&#39;t familiar with LDAP, this may be confusing so let&#39;s go into greater detail.</p>
  675. <p>For LDAP to function, objects in AD must be formatted according to a specific naming standard. To show an example of a DN, we can use our <code>stephanie</code> domain user. We know that <code>stephanie</code> is a user object in <code>corp.com</code> domain. The DN may, though we cannot be sure yet, look like this:</p>
  676. <pre><code>CN=Stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  677. </code></pre>
  678. <ul>
  679. <li>CN (Common Name)</li>
  680. <li>Specifies the identifier of an object in the domain.</li>
  681. <li>DC (Domain Component)</li>
  682. <li>In AD terms DC is Domain Controller, but when refereing to a DN, DC means Domain Component.</li>
  683. <li>Represents the top of an LDAP tree, in this case it is the DN of the domain itself.</li>
  684. </ul>
  685. <p>When reading a DN, we start with the DC objects on the right side and move to the left. In this case, we have 4 components, starting with two components names <code>DC=corp</code>, <code>DC=com</code>. The Domain Component objects mentioned above are the top of an LDAP tree following the required naming standard.</p>
  686. <p>The next DN field, <code>CN=Users</code> respresents the common name for the container where user object is stored, aka the parent container.</p>
  687. <p>The left most field <code>CN=Stephanie</code> represents the common name for the user object itself, which is lowest in the hierarchy.</p>
  688. <p>In the case of the LDAP path we are interested in the Domain Component object, <code>DC=corp</code> and <code>DC=com</code>. If we add <code>CN=Users</code> to our LDAP path we would be restricted to searching onjects within the given container.</p>
  689. <p>Let&#39;s begin writing our script by obtaining the required hostname for the PDC.</p>
  690. <p>In the MS .NET classes relating to AD we will find the <code>System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory</code> namespace. We will focus on the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.activedirectory.domain?view=windowsdesktop-7.0">Domain Class</a>, but there are several classes to choose from. It contains a reference to the <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> in the properties. We find a method called <code>GetCurrentDomain()</code> which returns the domain object for the current user, <code>stephanie</code> in this case.</p>
  691. <p>To invoke <code>Domain Class</code> and <code>GetCurrentDomain()</code> we run the following command in PowerShell.</p>
  692. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
  693. ​
  694. ​
  695. Forest : corp.com
  696. DomainControllers : {DC1.corp.com}
  697. Children : {}
  698. DomainMode : Unknown
  699. DomainModeLevel : 7
  700. Parent :
  701. PdcRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  702. RidRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  703. InfrastructureRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  704. Name : corp.com
  705. </code></pre>
  706. <ul>
  707. <li>From the output we see <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> prop is <code>DC1.corp.com</code></li>
  708. </ul>
  709. <p>We could add the hostname directly into our script as part of the LDAP path, but we want to automate the process so we can also use this script in future engagements.</p>
  710. <p>First we create a var that will store the domain object, then we will print the variable so we can verfiy that it still works in our script.</p>
  711. <pre><code># Store the domain object in the $domainObj variable
  712. $domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
  713. ​
  714. # Print the variable
  715. $domainObj
  716. </code></pre>
  717. <p>We must bypass execution policy to run our script with <code>powershell -ep bypass</code></p>
  718. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; powershell.exe -ep bypass
  719. Windows PowerShell
  720. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  721. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  722. Forest : corp.com
  723. DomainControllers : {DC1.corp.com}
  724. Children : {}
  725. DomainMode : Unknown
  726. DomainModeLevel : 7
  727. Parent :
  728. PdcRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  729. RidRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  730. InfrastructureRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  731. Name : corp.com
  732. </code></pre>
  733. <p>Our <code>domainObj</code> var now holds the info about the domain object, the print statement verifies that our command and var work as expected.</p>
  734. <p>Since the hostname in the <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> prop is required for our LDAP path, we can extract the name directly from the domain object. In case we need more info from the domain object later in our script, we will keep the <code>$domainObj</code> for the time being and create a new variable called <code>$PDC</code>, which will extract the val from the <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> prop held in <code>$domainObj</code> var.</p>
  735. <pre><code># Store the domain object in the $domainObj variable
  736. $domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
  737. ​
  738. # Store the PdcRoleOwner name to the $PDC variable
  739. $PDC = $domainObj.PdcRoleOwner.Name
  740. ​
  741. # Print the $PDC variable
  742. $PDC
  743. </code></pre>
  744. <p>Running the script again.</p>
  745. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  746. DC1.corp.com
  747. </code></pre>
  748. <p>In this case we have dynamically extracted the PDC from the <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> prop using Domain Class.</p>
  749. <p>We can also get the DN for the domain via the domain object, but it doesn&#39;t follow the LDAP naming standard. We know that the base domain is <code>corp.com</code> and the DN would be <code>DC=corp</code>,<code>DC=com</code>. We could grap <code>corp.com</code> from the Name prop in the domain object and tell PowerShell to break it up and add the <code>DC=</code> param. However there is an easier way which assures we obtain the correct DN.</p>
  750. <p>We can use ADSI directly in PS to retrieve the DN. Use two single quotes to indicate that the search starts at the top of the AD hierarchy.</p>
  751. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  752. DC=corp,DC=com
  753. </code></pre>
  754. <ul>
  755. <li>Returns the DN in LDAP path format.</li>
  756. </ul>
  757. <p>We can add a new var in our script that will store the Dn for the new domain. </p>
  758. <pre><code># Store the domain object in the $domainObj variable
  759. $domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
  760. ​
  761. # Store the PdcRoleOwner name to the $PDC variable
  762. $PDC = $domainObj.PdcRoleOwner.Name
  763. ​
  764. # Print the $PDC variable
  765. $PDC
  766. ​
  767. # Store the Distinguished Name variable into the $DN variable
  768. $DN = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  769. ​
  770. # Print the $DN variable
  771. $DN
  772. </code></pre>
  773. <p>Run our script.</p>
  774. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  775. DC1.corp.com
  776. DC=corp,DC=com
  777. </code></pre>
  778. <ul>
  779. <li>We dynamically obtain the Hostname and DN with our script.</li>
  780. </ul>
  781. <p>Now we must assemble the pieves to build the full LDAP path. We need to add a new <code>$LDAP</code> var that will contain the prior vars prefixed with <code>LDAP://</code>.</p>
  782. <p>We can condense the code adding <code>PdcRoleOwner</code> to <code>$PDC</code> on the first line and remove the comments.</p>
  783. <pre><code>$PDC = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain().PdcRoleOwner.Name
  784. $DN = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  785. $LDAP = &quot;LDAP://$PDC/$DN&quot;
  786. $LDAP
  787. </code></pre>
  788. <p>Run our script.</p>
  789. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  790. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/DC=corp,DC=com
  791. </code></pre>
  792. <ul>
  793. <li>We succesfully used .NET classes and ADSI to dynamically obtain the full LDAP path required for enum.</li>
  794. <li>This script can be easily resused in real-world.</li>
  795. </ul>
  796. <h5>Adding Search Functionality to our Script</h5>
  797. <p>Now that our script builds the LDAP path we can build in our search function.</p>
  798. <p>We need two .NET classes located in the <code>System.DiretoryServices</code> namespace.</p>
  799. <ul>
  800. <li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.directoryentry?view=dotnet-plat-ext-6.0">DirectoryEntry</a></li>
  801. <li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.directorysearcher?view=dotnet-plat-ext-6.0">DirectorySearcher</a></li>
  802. </ul>
  803. <p><code>DirectoryEntry</code> class encapsulates an object in the AD service hierarchy. In our case we will search from the top of the AD heirarchy by providing the LDAP path to the <code>DirectoyEntry</code> class.</p>
  804. <p><em>One thing to note with DirectoryEntry is that we can pass it credentials to authenticate to the domain. However, since we are already logged in, there is no need to do that here.</em></p>
  805. <p>The <code>DirectorySearcher</code> class queries against AD using LDAP, we must specify the AD service to query in the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.directoryservices.directorysearcher.searchroot?view=dotnet-plat-ext-6.0">SearchRoot</a> prop. According to MS docs, this prop indicated where search starts in AD hierarchy. Since the <code>DirectoryEntry</code> class encapsulates the LDAP path pointing to the top of the hierarchy we can pass that as a var to <code>DirectorySearcher</code>.</p>
  806. <p>The <code>DirectorySearcher</code> docs list <code>FindAll()</code> which returns all entries found in AD.</p>
  807. <p>Implement the two classes in our script.</p>
  808. <pre><code>$PDC = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain().PdcRoleOwner.Name
  809. $DN = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  810. $LDAP = &quot;LDAP://$PDC/$DN&quot;
  811. ​
  812. $direntry = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry($LDAP)
  813. ​
  814. $dirsearcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($direntry)
  815. $dirsearcher.FindAll()
  816. </code></pre>
  817. <ul>
  818. <li>We added the <code>$direntry</code> var.</li>
  819. <li>Encapsulates our LDAP path.</li>
  820. <li><code>$dirsearcher</code> var contains the <code>$direntry</code> var and uses the info as <code>SearchRoot</code> .</li>
  821. <li>Pointing to the top of the hierarchy where <code>DirectorySearcher</code> will run the <code>FindAll()</code> method.</li>
  822. </ul>
  823. <p>Since the search starts at the top and we aren&#39;t filtering results, it generates a lot fo output.</p>
  824. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  825. ​
  826. Path
  827. ----
  828. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/DC=corp,DC=com

  831. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/OU=Domain Controllers,DC=corp,DC=com

  847. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=AppCategories,CN=Default Domain Policy,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com
  848. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=Meetings,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com

  850. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN={31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com

  854. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=User,CN={6AC1786C-016F-11D2-945F-00C04fB984F9},CN=Policies,CN=System,DC=...

  856. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=RAS and IAS Servers Access Check,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com
  857. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=File Replication Service,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com
  858. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=Dfs-Configuration,CN=System,DC=corp,DC=com

  861. </code></pre>
  862. <ul>
  863. <li>We are receiving objects in the entire domain.</li>
  864. <li>This proves the script is working as expected.</li>
  865. </ul>
  866. <p>There are several simple ways to filter the output. We ca setup a filter on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/adschema/a-samaccounttype">samAccountType</a> attribute, which is applied to all user, computer, and group objects.</p>
  867. <p>The official docs reveal different values of the <code>samAccountType</code> attribute, but we start with <code>0x30000000</code> (decimal 805306368), which will enumerate all users in the domain. To implement the filter in our script, we can add the filter to the <code>$dirsearcher.filter</code> as shown below.</p>
  868. <pre><code>$PDC = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain().PdcRoleOwner.Name
  869. $DN = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  870. $LDAP = &quot;LDAP://$PDC/$DN&quot;
  871. ​
  872. $direntry = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry($LDAP)
  873. ​
  874. $dirsearcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($direntry)
  875. $dirsearcher.filter=&quot;samAccountType=805306368&quot;
  876. $dirsearcher.FindAll()
  877. </code></pre>
  878. <p>Running the script displays all user objects in the domain.</p>
  879. <pre><code>Path Properties

  885. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  886. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=jeff,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  887. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=jeffadmin,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  888. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=iis_service,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  889. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=pete,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  890. LDAP://DC1.corp.com/CN=jen,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com {logoncount, codepage, objectcateg...
  891. </code></pre>
  892. <p>Great info to have be we need to take it a little furhter. When we enum AD we are interested in the attributes of each object, store in the Properties field.</p>
  893. <p>We can store the results we receive in a new var, iterate through each object, and print each prop on its own line via a nested loop as shown.</p>
  894. <pre><code>$domainObj = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain()
  895. $PDC = $domainObj.PdcRoleOwner.Name
  896. $DN = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  897. $LDAP = &quot;LDAP://$PDC/$DN&quot;
  898. ​
  899. $direntry = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry($LDAP)
  900. ​
  901. $dirsearcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($direntry)
  902. $dirsearcher.filter=&quot;samAccountType=805306368&quot;
  903. $result = $dirsearcher.FindAll()
  904. ​
  905. Foreach($obj in $result)
  906. {
  907. Foreach($prop in $obj.Properties)
  908. {
  909. $prop
  910. }
  911. ​
  912. Write-Host &quot;-------------------------------&quot;
  913. }
  914. </code></pre>
  915. <ul>
  916. <li>Search through AD and filter results based on <code>samAccountType</code> of our choice and place it in the <code>$result</code> variable.</li>
  917. <li>Further filter the results based on two foreach loops.</li>
  918. <li>The first loop will extract the objects stored in <code>$result</code> and place them in the <code>$obj</code> var.</li>
  919. <li>The second loop extracts all properties for each object and store the info in the <code>$prop</code> var, outputing it to terminal.</li>
  920. </ul>
  921. <p>The <code>Write-Host</code> command is not required for the script to function but it does print a line between each object, making the output easier to read.</p>
  922. <p>The script outputs a lot of information, which can become overwhelming depending on the number of domain users. The listing below shows a partial view of <code>jeffeadmin</code> attributes.</p>

  958. <p>We can filter based on any prop of any object type. In the example below we make two changes. First we change the filter to use the <code>name</code> prop to only show info about <code>jeffadmin</code>. Secondly we added <code>.memberof</code> to the <code>$prop</code> var to only display the groups <code>jeffadmin</code> is a member of.</p>
  959. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; .\enum.ps1
  960. CN=Domain Admins,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  961. CN=Administrators,CN=Builtin,DC=corp,DC=com
  962. </code></pre>
  963. <ul>
  964. <li>Confirming <code>jeffadmin</code> is a member of <code>Domain Admins</code> group.</li>
  965. </ul>
  966. <p>We can use this script to enum any object available to us in AD, in the current state it would require us to make further edits to the script itself based on what we want to enum.</p>
  967. <p>We can instead make the script more flexible, allowing us to add the params to the CLI. We can have the script accept the <code>samAccountType</code> we wish to enum as a CLI arg.</p>
  968. <p>There are many ways to accomplish this, we can encapsulate the current functionality of the script into an actual function.</p>
  969. <pre><code>function LDAPSearch {
  970. param (
  971. [string]$LDAPQuery
  972. )
  973. ​
  974. $PDC = [System.DirectoryServices.ActiveDirectory.Domain]::GetCurrentDomain().PdcRoleOwner.Name
  975. $DistinguishedName = ([adsi]&#39;&#39;).distinguishedName
  976. ​
  977. $DirectoryEntry = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectoryEntry(&quot;LDAP://$PDC/$DistinguishedName&quot;)
  978. ​
  979. $DirectorySearcher = New-Object System.DirectoryServices.DirectorySearcher($DirectoryEntry, $LDAPQuery)
  980. ​
  981. return $DirectorySearcher.FindAll()
  982. ​
  983. }
  984. </code></pre>
  985. <ul>
  986. <li>At the top we declare the function with a name of our choosing.<ul>
  987. <li><code>LDAPSearch</code></li>
  988. </ul>
  989. </li>
  990. <li>We then dynamically obtain the required LDAP path connection string and add it to the <code>$DirectoryEntry</code> var.</li>
  991. <li>The <code>DirectoryEntry</code> and our <code>$LDAPQuery</code> param is fed into the <code>DirectorySearcher</code></li>
  992. <li>The search is run and output is added into an array.</li>
  993. <li>Displayed in terminal depening on our needs.</li>
  994. </ul>
  995. <p>To use the function import it into memory.</p>
  996. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; Import-Module .\function.ps1
  997. </code></pre>
  998. <p>In PowerShell we can now use the LDAPSearch command to obtain info from AD. To repear the user enum we did earlier, we can again filter on the <code>specificAccountType</code></p>
  999. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery &quot;(samAccountType=805306368)&quot;

  1038. <ul>
  1039. <li>The script enums more groups than <code>net.exe</code> including .<ul>
  1040. <li><code>Print Operators</code></li>
  1041. <li><code>ISS_IUSRS</code></li>
  1042. </ul>
  1043. </li>
  1044. <li>Etc.</li>
  1045. <li>It enums all objects of AD encluding Domain Local groups.</li>
  1046. <li>Not just global groups.</li>
  1047. </ul>
  1048. <p>To print props and attributes for objects we need to implement the loops we used earlier. We can do this directly from the PowerShell command.</p>
  1049. <p>To enum every group available in the domain and display user memebers we pipe output into a new var and use a <code>foreach</code> loop to print each prop of a given group. This allows us to select the attributes we want, let&#39;s focus on <code>CN</code> and <code>member</code> attributes.</p>
  1050. <pre><code>foreach ($group in $(LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery &quot;(objectCategory=group)&quot;)) { &gt;&gt; $group.properties | select {$_.cn}, {$_.member} &gt;&gt; }
  1051. </code></pre>
  1052. <p>Althought the env is small we still received a lot of output, focus on the three groups we noticed earlier in our enum with <code>net.exe</code>.</p>
  1053. <pre><code class="language-...">Sales Department {CN=Development Department,DC=corp,DC=com, CN=pete,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com, CN=stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com}
  1054. Management Department CN=jen,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1055. Development Department {CN=Management Department,DC=corp,DC=com, CN=pete,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com, CN=dave,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com}
  1056. ...
  1057. </code></pre>
  1058. <p>We have expanded teh props for each object, the group object in this case, and printed the member attributes for each group.</p>
  1059. <p>We reveal something unexpected, when we enum the <code>Sales Department</code> group earlier with <code>net.exe</code> we only found two users, <code>pete</code> and <code>stephanie</code>. In this case it appears that Development Department is also a member.</p>
  1060. <p>Since the output can be somewhat difficult to read we search from groups, but specify <code>Sales Department</code> in the query and pipe it to a var in our PS command line.</p>
  1061. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; $sales = LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery &quot;(&amp;(objectCategory=group)(cn=Sales Department))&quot;
  1062. </code></pre>
  1063. <p>Now that we have one object in our var, we can just print the member attribute directly.</p>
  1064. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; $sales.properties.member
  1065. CN=Development Department,DC=corp,DC=com
  1066. CN=pete,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1067. CN=stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1068. </code></pre>
  1069. <ul>
  1070. <li>The <code>Development Deparment</code> is indeed a member of the <code>Sales Department</code></li>
  1071. <li>Something we missed with <code>net.exe</code></li>
  1072. <li>This is a nested group.</li>
  1073. <li>Relatively common in AD and scales well.</li>
  1074. <li>Provides flexible and dynamic membership customization of large AD implementations.</li>
  1075. <li><code>net.exe</code> missed this because it only lists <code>user</code> objects, not group objects.</li>
  1076. <li>It can only display specific attributes, emphasizing the benefits of custom tools.</li>
  1077. </ul>
  1078. <p>Now that we know there is a nested group let&#39;s enum it.</p>
  1079. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; $group = LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery &quot;(&amp;(objectCategory=group)(cn=Development Department*))&quot;
  1080. PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; $group.properties.member
  1081. CN=Management Department,DC=corp,DC=com
  1082. CN=pete,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1083. CN=dave,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1084. </code></pre>
  1085. <ul>
  1086. <li>We find another nested group.<ul>
  1087. <li><code>Management Department</code></li>
  1088. </ul>
  1089. </li>
  1090. </ul>
  1091. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; $group = LDAPSearch -LDAPQuery &quot;(&amp;(objectCategory=group)(cn=Management Department*))&quot;
  1092. PS C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop&gt; $group.properties.member
  1093. CN=jen,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  1094. </code></pre>
  1095. <ul>
  1096. <li>After searching through multiple groups we found the end.</li>
  1097. <li><code>jen</code> is the sole member of <code>Management Department</code> group.</li>
  1098. </ul>
  1099. <p>Note that <code>jen</code> is only part of <code>Mangement Department</code> group, but she is also an indirect member Sales and Development groups, because groups inherit from each other. This is normal behaviour in AD, if misconfigured though users can end up with more privs than inteded! This can allow attackers to take advantage of the misconfig to expand their reach in the domain.</p>

  1194. <h5>AD Enumeration with PowerView</h5>
  1195. <p>So far we have only focused on enumerating users and groups. The tools we have used so far have given us a basic understanding of how to communicate with AD and<a href="https://powersploit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Recon/">PowerView</a> retrieve information, other researchers have created more advanced tools for this purpose.</p>
  1196. <p><a href="https://powersploit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Recon/">PowerView</a> PowerShell script is a popular option including many functions to improve the effectiveness of enumeration.</p>
  1197. <p>Let&#39;s get acquainted with PowerView by walking through our prior enumeration steps. PowerView is already installed in <code>C:\Tools</code> dir of CLIENT75. To use it we must first import it to memory.</p>
  1198. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
  1199. </code></pre>
  1200. <p>With the module imported we can explore the available commands. Refer to the linked reference for a list of all commands.</p>
  1201. <p>Start by running <code>Get-NetDomain</code> which gives us basic information about the domain (where we previously used GetCurrentDomain).</p>
  1202. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; Get-NetDomain
  1203. ​
  1204. ​
  1205. Forest : corp.com
  1206. DomainControllers : {DC1.corp.com}
  1207. Children : {}
  1208. DomainMode : Unknown
  1209. DomainModeLevel : 7
  1210. Parent :
  1211. PdcRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  1212. RidRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  1213. InfrastructureRoleOwner : DC1.corp.com
  1214. Name : corp.com
  1215. </code></pre>
  1216. <ul>
  1217. <li>PowerView uses .NET classes to obtain LDAP path and comm with AD.</li>
  1218. </ul>
  1219. <p>Let&#39;s get a list of all users in the domain with <code>Get-Netuser</code></p>
  1220. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; Get-NetUser
  1221. ​
  1222. ​
  1223. logoncount : 546

  1278. <ul>
  1279. <li><code>Get-NetUser</code> automatically enumerates all attributes on the user objects.</li>
  1280. <li>Producing a lot of info.</li>
  1281. </ul>
  1282. <p>In our script we used loops to print certain attributes based on the info obtained. With PowerView we can pipe the output into <code>select</code>, where we can choose specific attributes.</p>
  1283. <p>The <code>cn</code> attribute holds the username of the user, pipe the output to <code>select</code> and choose the <code>cn</code> attribute.</p>
  1284. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; Get-NetUser | select cn
  1285. ​
  1286. cn
  1287. --
  1288. Administrator
  1289. Guest
  1290. krbtgt
  1291. dave
  1292. stephanie
  1293. jeff
  1294. jeffadmin
  1295. iis_service
  1296. pete
  1297. jen
  1298. </code></pre>
  1299. <ul>
  1300. <li>Produced a cleaned up list of users in the domain.</li>
  1301. </ul>
  1302. <p>There are many interesting attributes to search for when enumerating AD. If a user is dormant, they have not changed their password or logged in recently, we will draw less attention if we take over the account during an engagement. Also, if a user hasn&#39;t changed their password since a recent password policy update, their password may be weaker than the current policy making it weaker to password attacks.</p>
  1303. <p>This can be easily investigated, run <code>Get-NetUser</code> again, piping the output to <code>select</code> and extracting the following attributes.</p>
  1304. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; Get-NetUser | select cn,pwdlastset,lastlogon
  1305. ​

  1686. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetComputer | select operatingsystem,dnshostname

  1750. <h5>Getting an Overview - Permissions and Logged on Users</h5>
  1751. <p>Now that we have a clear list of computers, users, and groups in the domain we continue enum focusing on the relationships between as many objects as possible. These relationships often play a key role during attack and our goal is to build a map of the domain to find attack vectors.</p>
  1752. <p>Example, when a user logs in to the domain their creds are cached in mem on the computer they logged in from.</p>
  1753. <p>If we can steal those creds we may be able to use them to auth as the domain user and potentially escalate our domain privs.</p>
  1754. <p>However during an AD assessment we may not always want to escalate privs right away.</p>
  1755. <p>It is more important to establish a good foothold and our goal is to maintain access. If we are able to compromise other users with the same perms as the user we already have access to, this allows us to maintain our foothold. Example, if the password is reset for the user we originally obtained access to or sys admin notices suspicious activity and disable the account, we would still have access to the domain via other users we compromised.</p>
  1756. <p>When it is time for PrivEsc we don&#39;t immediatly need domain admin because there may be other accounts that have higher privs than regular user even if they aren&#39;t part of Domain Admin group. Service Accounts, which we will discuss later, are a good example of this. Although they may not have the highest privs, they may have more perms than regular domain user, such as local admin privs on specific servers.</p>
  1757. <p>In addition an orgs most sensitive and important data may be stored in locations that do not require domain admin privs, a DB or file server for instance. Due to this, domain admin privs should not always be the end goal during an assesment since we may be able to reach the &quot;crown jewels&quot; for an org via other users in the domain.</p>
  1758. <p><em>Nevertheless, in our Challenge Labs the goal is to achieve domain administrator privileges.</em></p>
  1759. <p>When an attacker improves access through multiple higher-level accounts to reach the goad, it is known as &quot;chained compromise&quot;.</p>
  1760. <p>To find possible attack paths we need to learn more about our initial user and see what domain access they have. We also need to find out where other users are logged in.</p>
  1761. <p>PowerView&#39;s <code>Find-LocalAdminAccess</code> command scans the network in an attempt to determine if our current user has admin perms on any computers in the domain. The command relies on <code>OpenServiceW</code> <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsvc/nf-winsvc-openservicew">function</a>, which connects to Service Control Manager (SCM) of the target machines. The SCM maintains a DB of installed services and drivers on Win computers. PowerView will attempt to open this DB with the SC_MANAGER_ALL_ACCESS access right, wich requires admin privs, and if successful PowerView will deem that our current user has admin privs on the target.</p>
  1762. <p>Run <code>Find-LocalAdminAccess</code> against <code>corp.com</code>. The command supports params like <code>Computername</code> and <code>Credentials</code> but we will run it without params in this case since we are interested in enum all computers and we are already logged in as <code>stephanie</code>. Essentially, we are spraying the env to find possible local admin access on computers under our current context.</p>
  1763. <p><em>Depending on the size of the environment, it may take a few minutes for Find-LocalAdminAccess to finish.</em></p>
  1764. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; powershell -ep bypass
  1765. Windows PowerShell
  1766. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  1767. ​
  1768. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows
  1769. ​
  1770. PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; cd C:\Tools\
  1771. PS C:\Tools&gt; Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1
  1772. PS C:\Tools&gt; Find-LocalAdminAccess
  1773. client74.corp.com
  1774. </code></pre>
  1775. <ul>
  1776. <li>User <code>stephanie</code> had admin privs on CLIENT74.</li>
  1777. </ul>
  1778. <p>It is tempting to log into CLIENT74 and check perms, we should first zoom out and generalize.</p>
  1779. <p>Pentests can lead us in many different directions and while we should follow up on the many different paths, based on our interactions we should stick to our plan and maintain a disciplined approach.</p>
  1780. <p>Continue by visualizing how computers and users are connected to one another. The first step is to obtain info such as which users are logged into with computers.</p>
  1781. <p>Historically, the two best Win APIs that may still achieve these goals are <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/lmwksta/nf-lmwksta-netwkstauserenum">NetWkstaUserEnum</a> and <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/lmshare/nf-lmshare-netsessionenum">NetSessionEnum</a>. The former requires admin privs while the later does not. Win has undergone changes over the last few years, which may make the discovery of logged in user enum more difficult for us.</p>
  1782. <p>PowerView&#39;s <code>Get-NetSession</code> command users <code>NetWkstaUserEnum</code> and <code>NetSessionEnum</code> API under the hood. Let&#39;s try to run it against some fo the machines in the domain to see if we can find any logged in users.</p>
  1783. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; cd C:\Tools\

  1786. PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetSession -ComputerName web04

  1788. <ul>
  1789. <li>We received no output.</li>
  1790. <li>There may be no users logged into the machine.</li>
  1791. <li>Assure we aren&#39;t receiving error messages by adding <code>-Verbose</code></li>
  1792. </ul>

  1795. PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetSession -ComputerName web04 -Verbose
  1796. VERBOSE: [Get-NetSession] Error: Access is denied
  1797. </code></pre>
  1798. <ul>
  1799. <li>It appears <code>NetSessionEnum</code> does not work in this case.</li>
  1800. <li>We are not allowed to run the query, likey due to perms.</li>
  1801. </ul>
  1802. <p>We may have admin privs on CLIENT74 with <code>stephanie</code>, run it against the machine and inspect the results.</p>
  1803. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetSession -ComputerName client74
  1804. ​
  1805. ​
  1806. CName : \\192.168.214.75
  1807. UserName : stephanie
  1808. Time : 0
  1809. IdleTime : 0
  1810. ComputerName : client74
  1811. </code></pre>
  1812. <ul>
  1813. <li>Taking a closer look the output IP in CName doesn not match the IP address for CLIENT74.</li>
  1814. <li>It matches the IP of our current machine, CLIENT75.</li>
  1815. <li>We haven&#39;t spawned any sessions to 74 so something appears to be off.</li>
  1816. </ul>
  1817. <p>IRL engagement, or even Challenge Labs, we might accept that enum sessions with PowerView does not work and try a different tool, but let&#39;s use this as a learning opportunity and take a deeper dive into the NetSessionEnum API to see why it does not work in this case.</p>
  1818. <p>According to NetSessionEnum docs there are five query levels: <code>0,1,2,10,502</code>.</p>
  1819. <ul>
  1820. <li>Level 0 only returns the name of the computer establishing the session.</li>
  1821. <li>Level 1,2 return more info but require admin privs.</li>
  1822. <li>Level 10,502 return info such as name of the computer and name of the user establishing the connection.</li>
  1823. </ul>
  1824. <p>By default PowerView uses query level 10 with NetSessionEnum, which should return this info.</p>
  1825. <p>The perms required to enum sessions with <code>NetSessionEnum</code> are defined in the <code>SrvsvcSessionInfo</code> reg key located in the <code>HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\DefaultSecurity</code> hive.</p>
  1826. <p>We use the Win 11 machine we are currently logged in on to check the perms, it may have different perms than the other machines in the env, it may give us an idea of what is going on.</p>
  1827. <p>In order to view perms we use the PowerShell <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.security/get-acl?view=powershell-7.3">Get-Acl</a> cmdlet to retrieve the perms for the object we define with the <code>-Path</code> flag and print them in our PowerShell prompt.</p>
  1828. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-Acl -Path HKLM:SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\DefaultSecurity\ | fl

  1832. LanmanServer\DefaultSecurity\
  1833. Owner : NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
  1834. Group : NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
  1835. Access : BUILTIN\Users Allow ReadKey
  1836. BUILTIN\Administrators Allow FullControl
  1837. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM Allow FullControl
  1838. CREATOR OWNER Allow FullControl
  1839. APPLICATION PACKAGE AUTHORITY\ALL APPLICATION PACKAGES Allow ReadKey
  1840. S-1-15-3-1024-1065365936-1281604716-3511738428-1654721687-432734479-3232135806-4053264122
  1841. -3456934681 Allow ReadKey
  1842. Audit :
  1843. Sddl : O:SYG:SYD:AI(A;CIID;KR;;;BU)(A;CIID;KA;;;BA)(A;CIID;KA;;;SY)(A;CIIOID;KA;;;CO)(A;CIID;KR;
  1844. ;;AC)(A;CIID;KR;;;S-1-15-3-1024-1065365936-1281604716-3511738428-1654721687-432734479-323
  1845. 2135806-4053264122-3456934681)
  1846. </code></pre>
  1847. <ul>
  1848. <li><code>Access</code> reveals the groups and users that have either <code>FullControl</code> or <code>ReadKey</code></li>
  1849. <li>They can read the <code>SrvsvcSessionInfo</code> key itself.</li>
  1850. <li>Groups defined by sys do not allow NetSessionEnum to enum reg key from a remote standpoint.</li>
  1851. <li>BUILTIN.</li>
  1852. <li>NT AUTHORITY.</li>
  1853. <li>CREATOR OWNER.</li>
  1854. <li>APPLICATION PACKAGE AUTHORITY.</li>
  1855. <li>The string in the end of the output is a <code>capability SID</code></li>
  1856. <li>The MS docs refer to the exact SID in our output.</li>
  1857. <li>It is an unforgable token of authority that grants a Win component or a Universal Windows Application access to various resources.</li>
  1858. <li>However it will not allow remote access to the reg keys of interest.</li>
  1859. </ul>
  1860. <p>In older Win versions, which MS does not specify, Authenticated Users were allowed to access the reg hive and obtain info from the <code>SrvsvcSessionInfo</code> key. Following the least priv principle, regular domain users should not be able to access this info within the domain, likely part of the reason the perms for reg hive changed as well. Due to perms, we can be certain NetSessionEnum will not be able to retrieve the info on default Win 11.</p>
  1861. <p>Now we can get a better sense of the OS version in use, using <code>Net-GetComputer</code> and include the <code>operatingsystemversion</code> attribute.</p>
  1862. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetComputer | select dnshostname,operatingsystem,operatingsystemversion

  1866. DC1.corp.com Windows Server 2022 Standard 10.0 (20348)

  1869. client74.corp.com Windows 11 Pro 10.0 (22000)

  1873. <ul>
  1874. <li>As we discovered earlier Win 10 is the oldest OS in the env.</li>
  1875. <li>Based on output it run version 16299.</li>
  1876. <li>Known as build 1709.</li>
  1877. </ul>
  1878. <p>The MS docs are not clear when the change was made to the reg hive, but it appears to be around the release of this build. It also affects Win servers since Server 2019 build 1809. This creates an issue for us since we will be unable to use PowerView to build the domain map we had in mind.</p>
  1879. <p>Though <code>NetSessionEnum</code> does not work in this case, it&#39;s not uncommon to find older systems IRL so we should keep it in our toolkit.</p>
  1880. <p>Luckily there are other tools we can use, such as <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/psloggedon">PsLoggedOn</a> app from the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/">SysInternals Suite</a>. The docs state that <code>PsLoggedOn</code> will enumerate the reg keys under <code>HKEY_USERS</code> to retrieve the security identifiers (SID) of logged-in users and convert the SIDs to usernames. <code>PsLoggedOn</code> will also use the NetSessionEnum API to see who is logged on to the computer via resource shares.</p>
  1881. <p>However, <code>PsLoggedOn</code> relies on the Remote Registry service to scan associated keys which limits it. The Remote Registry service has not been enabled by default on Win workstations since Win 8, but sys admins may enable it for various admin tasks, backwards compatability, or for installing monitoring deploymnet tools, scripts, agents, etc.</p>
  1882. <p>It is also enabled by default on later Win Server OS systems (Server 2012 R2, 2016 (1607), 2019 (1809), Server 2022 (21H2)). If enabled the service will stop after ten minutes of inactivity to save resources, but will re-enable with an auto trigger once we connect with <code>PsLoggedOn</code>.</p>
  1883. <p>With the theory out of the way let&#39;s try to run <code>PsLoggedOn</code> against the computers we attempted to enum earlier, starting with FILES04/WEB04.</p>
  1884. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools\PSTools&gt; .\PsLoggedon.exe \\files04

  1973. <h5>Enumeration Through Service Principal Names</h5>
  1974. <p>At this point we have obtained a good bit of info and are starting to see how things are connected together within the domain. To complete our discussion on enum, we will shift our focus to <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/active-directory/fundamentals/service-accounts-on-premises">Service Accounts</a>, which can also be members of high priv groups.</p>
  1975. <p>Apps must exec inthe context of an OS user. If a user launches an app, the user account defines the context. Service launched by the system itself run in the context of a Service Account.</p>
  1976. <p>Isolated apps ca use a set of predefined service accounts.</p>
  1977. <ul>
  1978. <li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/services/localsystem-account">LocalSystem</a></li>
  1979. <li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/services/localservice-account">LocalService</a></li>
  1980. <li><a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/services/networkservice-account">NetworkService</a></li>
  1981. </ul>
  1982. <p>For more complex apps a domain user account may be used, providing the context while maintaining access to domain resources.</p>
  1983. <p>When apps like Exchange, MS SQL, or IIS are integrated into AD a unique Service Principal Name (SPN) associates a service to a specific service account in AD.</p>
  1984. <p><em>Managed Service Accounts, introduced with Windows Server 2008 R2, were designed for complex applications, which require tighter integration with Active Directory.</em></p>
  1985. <p><em>Larger applications like MS SQL and Microsoft Exchange often required server redundancy when running to guarantee availability, but Managed Service Accounts did not support this. To remedy this, Group Managed Service Accounts were introduced with Windows Server 2012, but this requires that domain controllers run Windows Server 2012 or higher. Because of this, some organizations may still rely on basic Service Accounts.</em></p>
  1986. <p>We can obtain IPs and port numbers of apps running on services integrated with AD by enuming the SPNs in the domain, therefore we do not need to run a broad port scan.</p>
  1987. <p>Since the info is registered and stored in AD, it is present on the DC. To obtain the data we query the DC for specific SPNs.</p>
  1988. <p>We have multiple options to enum the SPNs in the domain. In this case we use <code>setspn.exe</code>, installed on Win by default. We use <code>-L</code> to run against both servers and clients in the domain.</p>
  1989. <p>We could iterate through a list of domain users, but we previously dicsovered the <code>iis_service</code> user. We will start with that one.</p>
  1990. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; setspn.exe -L iis_service
  1991. Registered ServicePrincipalNames for CN=iis_service,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com:
  1992. HTTP/web04.corp.com
  1993. HTTP/web04
  1994. HTTP/web04.corp.com:80
  1995. </code></pre>
  1996. <ul>
  1997. <li>We find an SPN linked to the <code>iis_service</code> account.</li>
  1998. </ul>
  1999. <p>We can also enum SPNs with PowerView by enuming all the accounts in the domain. To obtain a clear list of SPNs, we can pipe the output into <code>select</code>, choosing <code>samaccountname</code> and <code>serviceprincipalname</code> attributes.</p>
  2000. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; powershell -ep bypass

  2008. ​

  2010. -------------- --------------------
  2011. krbtgt kadmin/changepw

  2014. <ul>
  2015. <li>We will explore the <code>krbtgt</code> account in upcoming AD modules.</li>
  2016. <li>The <code>serviceprincipalname</code> of <code>iis_service</code> is indicative of a web server.<ul>
  2017. <li><code>{HTTP/web04.corp.com, HTTP/web04, HTTP/web04.corp.com:80}</code></li>
  2018. </ul>
  2019. </li>
  2020. </ul>
  2021. <p>Let&#39;s attempt to resolve <code>web04.corp.com</code> with <code>nslookup</code>.</p>
  2022. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; nslookup.exe web04.corp.com
  2023. DNS request timed out.
  2024. timeout was 2 seconds.
  2025. Server: UnKnown
  2026. Address: 192.168.227.70
  2027. ​
  2028. Name: web04.corp.com
  2029. Address: 192.168.227.72
  2030. </code></pre>
  2031. <ul>
  2032. <li>The hostname resolves to an internal IP.</li>
  2033. <li>If we browse there we find a website that requires login.</li>
  2034. </ul>
  2035. <p>Since these accounts run services we can assume they have higher privs than regular domain user accounts. For now we document the SPN linked to <code>iis_service</code>, which will be valuable in upcoming modules.</p>
  2036. <h5>Enumerating Object Permissions</h5>
  2037. <p>Next we will enum specific perms associated with AD objects. The technical details of those perms are complex and beyond the scope of this module, but it is important that we discuss the basics.</p>
  2038. <p>Objects in AD can have a set of perms applied to them with multiple <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-control-entries">Access Control Entries (ACE)</a>, which make up the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-control-lists">Access Control List (ACL)</a>. Each ACE defines if access to an object is allowed or denied.</p>
  2039. <p>Example, a domain user attempts to access a domain share, which is an object. The targeted object, the share in this case, will go through a validation check based on the ACL to determine if the user has perms to the share. ACL validation involves two main steps.</p>
  2040. <ul>
  2041. <li>The user sends an access token.</li>
  2042. <li>Consists of user identity and permissions.</li>
  2043. <li>Target object validates the token against the list of perms (ACL)</li>
  2044. <li>If the ACL allows the user to access the share, access is granted.</li>
  2045. <li>Otherwise request is denied.</li>
  2046. </ul>
  2047. <p>AD includes numerous permission types which can be used to configure an ACE. From the attacking standpoint, we are mainly interested in several key permission types. Here is a short list of the interesting ones</p>
  2048. <pre><code>GenericAll: Full permissions on object
  2049. GenericWrite: Edit certain attributes on the object
  2050. WriteOwner: Change ownership of the object
  2051. WriteDACL: Edit ACE&#39;s applied to object
  2052. AllExtendedRights: Change password, reset password, etc.
  2053. ForceChangePassword: Password change for object
  2054. Self (Self-Membership): Add ourselves to for example a group
  2055. </code></pre>
  2056. <ul>
  2057. <li>Other permissions are described in the <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/secauthz/access-rights-and-access-masks">MS Docs</a></li>
  2058. </ul>
  2059. <p>We can use <code>Get-ObjectAcl</code> to enum ACEs with PowerView, let&#39;s enum our own user to determine which ACEs are applied to it and filter on <code>-Identity</code>:</p>
  2060. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-ObjectAcl -Identity stephanie
  2061. ​
  2062. ...
  2063. ObjectDN : CN=stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  2064. ObjectSID : S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-1104
  2065. ActiveDirectoryRights : ReadProperty
  2066. ObjectAceFlags : ObjectAceTypePresent
  2067. ObjectAceType : 4c164200-20c0-11d0-a768-00aa006e0529
  2068. InheritedObjectAceType : 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000
  2069. BinaryLength : 56
  2070. AceQualifier : AccessAllowed
  2071. IsCallback : False
  2072. OpaqueLength : 0
  2073. AccessMask : 16
  2074. SecurityIdentifier : S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-553
  2075. AceType : AccessAllowedObject
  2076. AceFlags : None
  2077. IsInherited : False
  2078. InheritanceFlags : None
  2079. PropagationFlags : None
  2080. AuditFlags : None
  2081. ...
  2082. </code></pre>
  2083. <ul>
  2084. <li>This may seem like an overwhemling amount of output, but we are primarily interested in:</li>
  2085. <li>ObjectSID.</li>
  2086. <li>ActiveDirectoryRights.</li>
  2087. <li>SecurityIdentifier.</li>
  2088. </ul>
  2089. <p>The output lists two <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/manage/understand-security-identifiers">Security Identifiers (SID)</a>, unique object values in AD. The first, in the ObjectSID prop, contains value</p>
  2090. <ul>
  2091. <li><code>S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-1104</code>
  2092. To make sense of the SID, we use PowerView&#39;s <code>Convert-SidToName</code> command to convert it to a domain object.</li>
  2093. </ul>
  2094. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Convert-SidToName S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-1104
  2095. CORP\stephanie
  2096. </code></pre>
  2097. <ul>
  2098. <li>The SID in the ObjectSID prop belongs to <code>stephanie</code> user (current)</li>
  2099. </ul>
  2100. <p>The ActiveDirectoryRIghts prop describes the perms applied to the object. To find out who has the ReadProperty perm, we convert the SecurityIdentifier value.</p>
  2101. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Convert-SidToName S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-553
  2102. CORP\RAS and IAS Servers
  2103. </code></pre>
  2104. <ul>
  2105. <li>The SID in SecurityIdentifier prop belongs to default AD group.</li>
  2106. <li>RAS and IAS Servers.</li>
  2107. </ul>
  2108. <p>Taking this info together we see that the RAS and IAS Servers group has ReadProperty access rights to our user. This is a common confiuration in AD and likely won&#39;t yield an attack vector, but we have used the exaple to make sense of the info we have obtained.</p>
  2109. <p>In general, we are interested in the <code>ActiveDirectoryRights</code> and <code>SecurityIdentifier</code> for each object we enumerate moving forward.</p>
  2110. <p>The highest access permissions we can have on an object is <code>GenericAll</code>. There are many interesting ones as we discussed previously, but we will use <code>GenericAll</code> as an example.</p>
  2111. <p>We can continue to use <code>Get-ObjectAcl</code> and select only the props we are interested in.</p>
  2112. <ul>
  2113. <li><code>ActiveDirectoryRights</code></li>
  2114. <li><code>SecurityIdentifier</code>
  2115. While <code>ObjectSID</code> is nice to have, it is unnecessary when enuming specific objects in AD since it will only contain the SID for the object we are enuming.</li>
  2116. </ul>
  2117. <p>We should enum all objects in the domain, but let&#39;s start with <code>Management Department</code> group. We will check if any users have <code>GenericAll</code> permissions.</p>
  2118. <p>To create manageable output we use the PS <code>-eq</code> flag to filter the <code>ActiveDirectoryRights</code> prop to only display values that equal <code>GenericAll</code>. Then we pipe the results into <code>select</code> and display only the <code>SecurityIdentifier</code> and <code>ActiveDirectoryRights</code> prop.</p>
  2119. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-ObjectAcl -Identity &quot;Management Department&quot; | ? {$_.ActiveDirectoryRights -eq &quot;GenericAll&quot;} | select SecurityIdentifier,ActiveDirectoryRights
  2120. ​
  2121. SecurityIdentifier ActiveDirectoryRights
  2122. ------------------ ---------------------
  2123. S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-512 GenericAll
  2124. S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-1104 GenericAll
  2125. S-1-5-32-548 GenericAll
  2126. S-1-5-18 GenericAll
  2127. S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-519 GenericAll
  2128. </code></pre>
  2129. <ul>
  2130. <li>We find a total of 5 objects with <code>GenericAll</code> perms in <code>Management Department</code></li>
  2131. </ul>
  2132. <p>Convert the SIDs into names.</p>
  2133. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; &quot;S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-512&quot;,&quot;S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-1104&quot;,&quot;S-1-5-32-548&quot;,&quot;S-1-5-18&quot;,&quot;S-1-5-21-1987370270-658905905-1781884369-519&quot; | Convert-SidToName
  2134. CORP\Domain Admins
  2135. CORP\stephanie
  2136. BUILTIN\Account Operators
  2137. Local System
  2138. CORP\Enterprise Admins
  2139. </code></pre>
  2140. <ul>
  2141. <li>The first belongs to <code>Domain Admins</code> group.</li>
  2142. <li>No surprise as Domain Admins have the highest privs in the domain.</li>
  2143. <li>It is interesting to find <code>stephanie</code> in that list.</li>
  2144. <li>Regular domain users should not have <code>GenericAll</code> so this may be a misconfig.</li>
  2145. </ul>
  2146. <p>This finding indicates <code>stephanie</code> is a powerful account, which is significant.</p>
  2147. <p>While ehuming the Management Group, we find <code>jen</code> is its only member. As an experiment to show the power of misconfig object perms, we will try to use out perms as <code>stephanie</code> to add ourselves to the group with <code>net.exe</code>.</p>
  2148. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; net group &quot;Management Department&quot; stephanie /add /domain
  2149. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  2150. ​
  2151. The command completed successfully.
  2152. </code></pre>
  2153. <ul>
  2154. <li>We should now be a member of the group.</li>
  2155. <li>Verify with <code>Get-NetGroup</code></li>
  2156. </ul>
  2157. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; net group &quot;Management Department&quot; stephanie /add /domain
  2158. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  2159. ​
  2160. The command completed successfully.
  2161. ​
  2162. PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetGroup &quot;Management Department&quot; | select member
  2163. ​
  2164. member
  2165. ------
  2166. {CN=jen,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com, CN=stephanie,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com}
  2167. </code></pre>
  2168. <ul>
  2169. <li>We see <code>jen</code> is no longer the sole member of the group.</li>
  2170. <li><code>stephanie</code> has been added.</li>
  2171. </ul>
  2172. <p>Now that we have abused <code>GenericAll</code> perm, use it to clean up after ourselves.</p>
  2173. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; net group &quot;Management Department&quot; stephanie /del /domain
  2174. The request will be processed at a domain controller for domain corp.com.
  2175. ​
  2176. The command completed successfully.
  2177. ​
  2178. PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-NetGroup &quot;Management Department&quot; | select member
  2179. ​
  2180. member
  2181. ------
  2182. CN=jen,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=com
  2183. </code></pre>
  2184. <ul>
  2185. <li>We see <code>jen</code> is once again the sole member of the group.</li>
  2186. </ul>
  2187. <p>From the perspective of a sys admin, managing AD perms can be a tough task, especially in complex envs. Weak perms, as we have seen here, are the go-to vectors for attackers since it can help us escalate privs in domain.</p>
  2188. <p>We enumed the Management Group object and leveraged <code>GenericAll</code> misconfig to add ourselved to the group.</p>
  2189. <h5>Enumerating Domain Shares</h5>
  2190. <p>Now we shift our focus to domain shares. Domain shares often contain critical info about the env, which we can use to our advantage.</p>
  2191. <p>We&#39;ll use PowerView&#39;s <code>Find-DomainShare</code> function to find the shares in the domain. We could add the <code>-CheckShareAccess</code> flag, displaying only shares available to us, but we will skip this for now to return a full list.</p>
  2192. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Import-Module .\PowerView.ps1

This share is generally used for domain policies and scripts. the <code>SYSVOL</code> folder is mapped to <code>%SystemRoot%\SYSVOL\Sysvol\domain-name</code> by default on the DC and every domain user has access to it.</p>

  2279. <ul>
  2280. <li>Note <code>cpassword=&quot;+bsY0V3d4/KgX3VJdO/vyepPfAN1zMFTiQDApgR92JE&quot;</code></li>
  2281. </ul>
  2282. <p>Due to the naming convention, it appears this is an older domain policy file. Domain admins often forget about them when implementing new policy, they are a common artifact. In this case the XML describes and old policy, helpful for learning about the new policies, and an encrypted password for the local built in admin account. The encrypted password could be extremely valuable.</p>
  2283. <p>Sys admins often change local workstation passwords through <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-server-2012-r2-and-2012/dn581922(v=ws.11)">Group Policy Preferences (GPP)</a>. </p>
  2284. <p>Although GPP-stored passwords are encrypted with AES-256, the private key for the encryption has been posted on <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/openspecs/windows_protocols/ms-gppref/2c15cbf0-f086-4c74-8b70-1f2fa45dd4be?redirectedfrom=MSDN#endNote2">MSDN</a>. We can use the key to decrypt these passwords, we will use <code>gpp-decrypt</code> Ruby script in Kali.</p>
  2285. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec]
  2286. └─$ gpp-decrypt &quot;+bsY0V3d4/KgX3VJdO/vyepPfAN1zMFTiQDApgR92JE&quot;
  2287. P@$$w0rd
  2288. ```bash
  2289. ​
  2290. - We successfullly decrypt the password and make note of `P@$$w0rd`

  2350. </code></pre>
  2351. <p>According to the file, <code>jeff</code> stored an email with a possible cleartext password, <code>HenchmanPutridConcon11!</code>. The password may have been changed, but we make not of it. With this and the password we collected earlier we are building a rough profile of the password policy for users/computers in the org. We can use this to create wordlists for password brute forcing, if needed.</p>
