  2410. <h4>5. Active Directory - Automated Enumeration</h4>
  2411. <ul>
  2412. <li>Collect domain data using SharpHound.</li>
  2413. <li>Analyze the data using BloodHound.</li>
  2414. </ul>
  2415. <p>Some automated tools, like <a href="https://www.pingcastle.com/">PingCastle</a>, generate gorgeous reports although most require paid licenses for commercial use. In our case, we will focus on <a href="https://bloodhound.readthedocs.io/en/latest/">BloodHound</a>, an excellent free tool that&#39;s extremely useful for analyzing AD environments.</p>
  2416. <p>It&#39;s worth noting that automated tools generate a great deal of network traffic and many administrators will likely recognize a spike in traffic as we run these tools.</p>
  2417. <h5>Collecting Data with SharpHound</h5>
  2418. <p>In the next section we will use BloodHound to analyze, sort, and present data, and us the companion tool <a href="https://bloodhound.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data-collection/sharphound.html">SharpHound</a> to collect the data. Sharphound is written in C# and uses Windows API functions with LDAP namespace functions similar to those we manually used in prior sections. Example, SharpHound will attempt to use <code>NetWkstaUserEnum</code> and <code>NetSessionEnum</code> to enum logged-on sessions, as we did earlier. It will also run queries agains the Remote Registry service, that we leveraged earlier.</p>
  2419. <p><em>It&#39;s often best to combine automatic and manual enumeration techniques when assessing Active Directory. Even though we could theoretically gather the same information with a manual approach, graphical relationships often reveal otherwise unnoticed attack paths.</em></p>
  2420. <p>First we need to get SharpHound up and running, it is available in several formats. We can compile it ourselves, use a precompiled bin, or use it as a PowerShell script. In this case, we will use the PowerShell script located in <code>C:\Tools</code> of CLIENT75. Let&#39;s open a PowerShell session and import the script.</p>
  2421. <p>We can now start collecting domain data. In order to run SharpHound, we must first run <code>Invoke-BloodHound</code>, which isn&#39;t intuitive since we&#39;re only running SharpHound. Use <code>Get-Help</code> to learn more about the command.</p>
  2422. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; powershell -ep bypass
  2423. Windows PowerShell
  2424. Copyright (C) Microsoft Corporation. All rights reserved.
  2425. ​
  2426. Install the latest PowerShell for new features and improvements! https://aka.ms/PSWindows
  2427. ​
  2428. PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; cd C:\Tools\
  2429. PS C:\Tools&gt; Import-Module .\SharpHound.ps1
  2430. PS C:\Tools&gt; Get-Help Invoke-BloodHound
  2431. ​
  2432. NAME
  2433. Invoke-BloodHound
  2434. ​
  2435. SYNOPSIS
  2436. Runs the BloodHound C# Ingestor using reflection. The assembly is stored in this file.
  2437. ​
  2438. ​
  2439. SYNTAX
  2440. Invoke-BloodHound [-CollectionMethods &lt;String[]&gt;] [-Domain &lt;String&gt;] [-SearchForest]
  2441. [-Stealth] [-LdapFilter &lt;String&gt;] [-DistinguishedName &lt;String&gt;] [-ComputerFile &lt;String&gt;]
  2442. [-OutputDirectory &lt;String&gt;] [-OutputPrefix &lt;String&gt;] [-CacheName &lt;String&gt;] [-MemCache]
  2443. [-RebuildCache] [-RandomFilenames] [-ZipFilename &lt;String&gt;] [-NoZip] [-ZipPassword &lt;String&gt;]
  2444. [-TrackComputerCalls] [-PrettyPrint] [-LdapUsername &lt;String&gt;] [-LdapPassword &lt;String&gt;]
  2445. [-DomainController &lt;String&gt;] [-LdapPort &lt;Int32&gt;] [-SecureLdap] [-DisableCertVerification]
  2446. [-DisableSigning] [-SkipPortCheck] [-PortCheckTimeout &lt;Int32&gt;] [-SkipPasswordCheck]
  2447. [-ExcludeDCs] [-Throttle &lt;Int32&gt;] [-Jitter &lt;Int32&gt;] [-Threads &lt;Int32&gt;]
  2448. [-SkipRegistryLoggedOn] [-OverrideUsername &lt;String&gt;] [-RealDNSName &lt;String&gt;]
  2449. [-CollectAllProperties] [-Loop] [-LoopDuration &lt;String&gt;] [-LoopInterval &lt;String&gt;]
  2450. [-StatusInterval &lt;Int32&gt;] [-Verbosity &lt;Int32&gt;] [-Help] [-Version] [&lt;CommonParameters&gt;]
  2451. ​
  2452. ​
  2453. DESCRIPTION
  2454. Using reflection and assembly.load, load the compiled BloodHound C# ingestor into memory
  2455. and run it without touching disk. Parameters are converted to the equivalent CLI arguments
  2456. for the SharpHound executable and passed in via reflection. The appropriate function
  2457. calls are made in order to ensure that assembly dependencies are loaded properly.
  2458. ​
  2459. ​
  2460. RELATED LINKS
  2461. ​
  2462. REMARKS
  2463. To see the examples, type: &quot;get-help Invoke-BloodHound -examples&quot;.
  2464. For more information, type: &quot;get-help Invoke-BloodHound -detailed&quot;.
  2465. For technical information, type: &quot;get-help Invoke-BloodHound -full&quot;.
  2466. </code></pre>
  2467. <p>We start with the <code>-CollectionMethod</code>, which describes the various <a href="https://bloodhound.readthedocs.io/en/latest/data-collection/sharphound-all-flags.html">collection methods</a>. We&#39;ll attempt to gather all data, which will perform all collection methods except for local group policies.</p>
  2468. <p>SharpHound will gather data in JSON files, automatically zipping them, by default which makes it easier to transfer files to Kali. Save the output file on our desktop with the &quot;corp audit&quot; prefix as shown below.</p>
  2469. <p>Data collection may tabke a few minutes, depending on the size of the env. Let&#39;s examine the output.</p>
  2470. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; Invoke-BloodHound -CollectionMethod All -OutputDirectory C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop\ -OutputPrefix &quot;corp audit&quot;

  2492. <ul>
  2493. <li>We scanned a total of 106 objects.</li>
  2494. <li>Varies based on objects and sessions in the domain.</li>
  2495. </ul>
  2496. <p>SharpHound took a &quot;snapshot&quot; of the domain from the <code>stephanie</code> user, allowing us to analyze everything the user account has access to. The data is store in a zip file on the user&#39;s desktop.</p>
  2497. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Tools&gt; ls C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop\
  2498. ​
  2499. ​
  2500. Directory: C:\Users\stephanie\Desktop
  2501. ​
  2502. ​
  2503. Mode LastWriteTime Length Name
  2504. ---- ------------- ------ ----
  2505. -a---- 12/6/2023 7:20 AM 12752 corp audit_20231206072020_BloodHound.zip
  2506. -a---- 12/6/2023 7:20 AM 9689 MTk2MmZkNjItY2IyNC00MWMzLTk5YzMtM2E1ZDcwYThkMzRl
  2507. .bin
  2508. </code></pre>
  2509. <ul>
  2510. <li>We&#39;ll us this file in the next section as we analyze the data with BloodHound.</li>
  2511. <li>SharpHound created a bin cache file to speed up data collection.</li>
  2512. <li>This is not needed for analysis and we can delete it.</li>
  2513. </ul>
  2514. <p>Note that SharpHound also supports looping, which has the collector run cyclical queries of our choice over a given period of time. The method we used above created a snapshot of the domain, running it in a loop can gather additional info as the env changes. The cache file speeds up the process. Example, if a user logged on after we created our snapshot we would have missed it. We will not use the loop func here, but recommend experimenting with it in training labs and inspecting hte results in BloodHound.</p>
  2515. <h5>Analysing Data using BloodHound</h5>
  2516. <p>In this section we will analyze the domain data using BloodHound in Kali, it should be noted that we can install the app and deps on Win systems as well.</p>
  2517. <p>To use BloodHound, we need to start the <a href="https://neo4j.com/">Neo4j</a> service, which is installed by default. Note, when BloodHound is installed with APT, the Neo4j service is automatically installed.</p>
  2518. <p>Neo4j is an open source graph DB (NoSQL) that creates nodes, edges, and properties instead of simple rows and columns. This visualizes our collected data, start the Neo4j service.</p>
  2519. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec]
  2520. └─$ sudo neo4j start
  2521. Directories in use:
  2522. home: /usr/share/neo4j
  2523. config: /usr/share/neo4j/conf
  2524. logs: /etc/neo4j/logs
  2525. plugins: /usr/share/neo4j/plugins
  2526. import: /usr/share/neo4j/import
  2527. data: /etc/neo4j/data
  2528. certificates: /usr/share/neo4j/certificates
  2529. licenses: /usr/share/neo4j/licenses
  2530. run: /var/lib/neo4j/run
  2531. Starting Neo4j.
  2532. Started neo4j (pid:334850). It is available at http://localhost:7474
  2533. There may be a short delay until the server is ready.
  2534. </code></pre>
  2535. <ul>
  2536. <li>The Neo4j service is now running and available at <code>http://localhost:7474</code></li>
  2537. <li>Default creds <code>neo4j/neo4j</code></li>
  2538. <li>Browse to Neo4j.</li>
  2539. <li>Login with default creds.</li>
  2540. <li>We are prompted to set a new password.</li>
  2541. <li>Note the password as we will use it to auth to the DB later.</li>
  2542. <li>New creds <code>neo4j/neotoor</code></li>
  2543. </ul>
  2544. <p>We can now auth to the DB and run our own queries against it. Since we haven&#39;t imported any data yet there isn&#39;t much we can do and we would prefer to let BloodHound run the queries for us.</p>
  2545. <p>With Neo4j running, start BloodHound.</p>
  2546. <pre><code class="language-bash">┌──(operator㉿labhost)-[~/OffSec]
  2547. └─$ bloodhound
  2548. </code></pre>
  2549. <ul>
  2550. <li>Once started, log in to the Neo4j DB.</li>
  2551. <li>The green check mark in the first col indicates BlooHound has detected the running Neo4j DB.</li>
  2552. </ul>
  2553. <p>We don&#39;t have any visual data yet as we haven&#39;t imported anything. To import the data we must first transfer the data zip from our Win machine to Kali. </p>
  2554. <pre><code class="language-powershell">PS C:\Users\stephanie&gt; scp &#39;.\Desktop\corp audit_20231207063037_BloodHound.zip&#39; admin@192.168.45.174:~/
  2555. admin@192.168.45.174&#39;s password:
  2556. corp audit_20231207063037_BloodHound.zip 100% 12KB 157.9KB/s 00:00
  2557. </code></pre>
  2558. <p>We then use the <code>Upload Data</code> func on the right side of the GUI to upload the Zip, or drap and drop it into the main window of BloodHound. Either way, the progress bar indicates the upload progress. Once finished, we can close the upload progress window.</p>
  2559. <p>Now we can start analyzing data. Let&#39;s get a sense of how much data is in the DB. Click the &quot;More Info&quot; tab in the top-left of the window. Our env is small and doesn&#39;t contain much, but in larger envs the DB may take some time to update. In those cases we can use the &quot;Refresh Database Stats&quot; button to present an updated view.</p>
  2560. <p>From our info, we have discovered 4 total sessions in the domain, enumed using <code>NetSessionEnum</code> and <code>PsLoggedOn</code>. We have discovered numerous ACLs, total of 10 users, 57 groups, and more.</p>
  2561. <p>We&#39;ll talk about &quot;Node Info&quot; later, there isn&#39;t much there ATM. We are mostly interested in the &quot;Analysis&quot; button at this point. Clicking it, we are presented with various pre-built options.</p>
  2562. <p>There are many pre-built queries, to get started we will use the &quot;Find all Domain Admins&quot; under &quot;Domain Information&quot;.
  2563. <img src="assets/static/resources/598a826b218c0697f9e9e39082ffa0e9.png" alt="598a826b218c0697f9e9e39082ffa0e9.png"></p>
  2564. <p>We are presented with the map below.
  2565. <img src="assets/static/resources/85b98c8defdefd88688fbe43d08d2017.png" alt="85b98c8defdefd88688fbe43d08d2017.png"></p>
  2566. <p>Each of the cirlce icons are known as a nodes, we can drag them and move them in the iface. We see 3 connected nodes, Bloodhound placed them far from eachother, so we can drag them closer to keep things tidy.</p>
  2567. <p><img src="assets/static/resources/822162ae5b6026ef37c2082ec1ca04af.png" alt="822162ae5b6026ef37c2082ec1ca04af.png">
  2568. To see what the 2 left nodes represent we can hover over them or toggle info by pressing <code>ctrl</code>. We can tell BloodHound how to show this info by clicking settings on the right side of the iface and setting Node Label Display to Always Display:
  2569. <img src="assets/static/resources/a65f311584791543037dc4f3ff2c7a92.png" alt="a65f311584791543037dc4f3ff2c7a92.png"></p>
  2570. <p>Based on this view the domain admins are:</p>
  2571. <ul>
  2572. <li><code>jeffadmin</code></li>
  2573. <li><code>administrator</code>
  2574. BloodHound shows an edge in the form of a line between the user objects and <code>Domain Admins</code> group object, indicating the relation that the users are a member of the group.</li>
  2575. </ul>
  2576. <p>BloodHound is capable of deep analysis, but much of its capability is out of the scope of this module. For now, focus on the Shortest Paths shown in the analysis tab.</p>
  2577. <p>Starting with &quot;Find Shortes Paths to Domain Admins&quot; as it provides a good overview without any params.
  2578. <img src="assets/static/resources/7aa8d6a247ad7d0eb3114c85fc819c24.png" alt="7aa8d6a247ad7d0eb3114c85fc819c24.png"></p>
  2579. <p>We can analyze the BloodHound graphs to determine the most effictient attack vector, the graph reveals a few things we missed in our ealier enum.</p>
  2580. <p>Let&#39;s focus on the <code>stephanie</code>/CLIENT74 relationship for now, Hover the mouse over the connecting strings between nodes to see the connection type.
  2581. <img src="assets/static/resources/fd64c13fe6d0cd82655c2c2a39ef5bad.png" alt="fd64c13fe6d0cd82655c2c2a39ef5bad.png"></p>
  2582. <p>We see <code>stephanie</code> has admin privs on CLIENT74. If we right click the line and select &quot;? Help&quot; we see addt info.
  2583. <img src="assets/static/resources/9fe295f4d34568203f9f1da634a0c701.png" alt="9fe295f4d34568203f9f1da634a0c701.png"></p>
  2584. <p>As we see, <code>stephanie</code> has several ways to obtain code exec on CLIENT74.</p>
  2585. <p><em>In the ? Help menu BloodHound also offers information in the Abuse tab, which will tell us more about the possible attack we can take on the given path. It also contains Opsec information as what to look out for when it comes to being detected, as well as references to the information displayed.</em></p>
  2586. <p>After further analysis we see that <code>jeffadmin</code> has a connection to CLIENT74, so there may be cached credentials on the machine. This could be critical, allowing us to steal admin creds and become domain admin.</p>
  2587. <p>This ties into the second &quot;Shortest Path&quot; for this module, the &quot;Shortes Paths to Domain Admins from Owned Principals&quot; query. If we run this against <code>corp.com</code> without configuring BloodHound we receive message &quot;NO DATA RETURNED FROM QUERY&quot;.</p>
  2588. <p>The &quot;Owned Principals&quot; is important, refering to objects we currently control in the domain. To analyze we mark objects as &quot;owned&quot; in BloodHound, even if we don&#39;t have access to them yet, it is good to think in terms of &quot;what if?&quot; when assessing AD. In this case we will focus on objects that we do in fact control.</p>
  2589. <p>We know that we control the <code>stephanie</code> user with partial control over CLIENT75, since we are logged in. We do not have admin privs, we need to link about PrivEsc later, but for now say we have control over it.</p>
  2590. <p>To obtain &quot;owned principal&quot; in BloodHound, we run a search on top left, right click the object that shows in the middle of the screen, and click &quot;Mark User as Owned&quot;. Owned principals show in BloodHound with a skull icon next to the node.
  2591. <img src="assets/static/resources/06af27f7a88df78094801e5517c81b79.png" alt="06af27f7a88df78094801e5517c81b79.png"></p>
  2592. <p>Not that if we click the icon for the object we are searching, it will be places into the &quot;node Info&quot; button where we can see details of the object itself.</p>
  2593. <p>Repeat the process for CLIENT75, clicking &quot;Mark Computer as Owned&quot; and we end up having two &quot;owned principals&quot;. Now we can run the &quot;Shortes Paths to Domain Admins from Owned Principals&quot; query.
  2594. <em>It&#39;s a good idea to mark every object we have access to as owned to improve our visibility into more potential attack vectors. There may be a short path to our goals that hinges on ownership of a particular object.</em>
  2595. <img src="assets/static/resources/a6f6676ec4e486b7e88aa31168179e17.png" alt="a6f6676ec4e486b7e88aa31168179e17.png"></p>
  2596. <ul>
  2597. <li>Note that we rearranged the nodes for clarity.</li>
  2598. </ul>
  2599. <p>Read starting from the left hand node, CLIENT75. User <code>stephanie</code> has a session there and should be able to connect to CLIENT74 where <code>jeffadmin</code> has a session, who is part of domain admin group. If we are able to take contorl of his account through impersonation or stealing creds on CLIENT74 we become domain admin.</p>
  2600. <p>While we focused on shortest paths, we highly recomend getting accustomed to the BloodHound pre-built queries withing the Challenge Labs.</p>
  2601. <p>In this domain, we were able to enum most info using manual methods, but in a large scale env with 1000s of users/computers this can be hard to digest. The queries from SharpHound generate noise in the network that will likely be caught by security analysis, it is a tool worth utilizing if the situation permits as it visualizes the findings for us.</p>
  2602. ​
  2603. </div>
  2604. </article>
